L1.T1.A1.skill_title: Find the resultant of perpendicular vectors and resolve a vector into components

items.question: What is the resultant of two vectors?
items.expectedAnswer: The single vector that has the same effect as the vectors combined.
items.explanation: The resultant is one vector equivalent in effect to all the vectors added together.
options: The single vector that has the same effect as the vectors combined.
The average of the two vectors.

items.question: Which method finds the magnitude of the resultant of two PERPENDICULAR vectors?
items.explanation: Perpendicular vectors form a right angle, so the resultant magnitude uses Pythagoras.

items.question: A force of 3 N east and 4 N north act on a point. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
A vector of magnitude 10 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component? (cos30° = 0.866)
items.explanation: Horizontal component = Fcosθ = 10 × cos30° = 8.66 N.

items.question: A vector of magnitude 10 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. What is its vertical component? (sin30° = 0.5)
items.explanation: Vertical component = Fsinθ = 10 × sin30° = 5 N.

items.question: Why must the direction of a resultant always be stated?
items.expectedAnswer: Because a resultant is a vector, which needs magnitude and direction.
items.explanation: A resultant is a vector; without a direction it is incomplete.
options: Because the magnitude is always unknown.
Because a resultant is a vector, which needs magnitude and direction.

items.question: Two perpendicular forces, 6 N and 8 N, act on a body. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
When you resolve a single vector into perpendicular components, the components are...
items.expectedAnswer: always smaller than the original vector.
items.explanation: Components are projections, so each is smaller than (or equal to) the original vector.
options: always larger than the original vector.
always smaller than the original vector.
equal to the original vector each.

items.question: Two perpendicular displacements, 5 m and 12 m, are added. What is the magnitude of the resultant displacement?
A velocity vector points due east. What is its component in the north direction?
items.explanation: A vector along east has no north component (the perpendicular component is zero).

items.question: Two perpendicular forces of 9 N and 12 N act on an object. Find the magnitude of the resultant.
A resultant force of 5 N acts east and 5 N acts north on an object. What angle does the resultant make with the east direction?
items.explanation: tanθ = opposite/adjacent = 5/5 = 1, so θ = 45°.

items.question: A box is pulled with a 20 N force at 60° to the horizontal. What is the horizontal component? (cos60° = 0.5)
items.explanation: Horizontal = Fcosθ = 20 × cos60° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N.

items.question: A box is pulled with a 20 N force at 60° to the horizontal. What is the vertical component? (sin60° = 0.866)
items.explanation: Vertical = Fsinθ = 20 × sin60° = 20 × 0.866 = 17.3 N.

items.question: Two perpendicular forces give a resultant of magnitude 10 N. If one force is 6 N, what is the other?
items.explanation: R² = Ax² + Ay² ⇒ 10² = 6² + Ay² ⇒ Ay² = 100 − 36 = 64 ⇒ Ay = 8 N.

items.question: Why can two perpendicular 3 N forces NOT give a 6 N resultant?
items.expectedAnswer: Perpendicular vectors add by Pythagoras, giving √(3²+3²) ≈ 4.24 N, not 6 N.
items.explanation: Only parallel vectors add directly; perpendicular ones combine via Pythagoras (≈ 4.24 N).
options: Perpendicular vectors add by Pythagoras, giving √(3²+3²) ≈ 4.24 N, not 6 N.

items.question: A plane flies at 100 m·s⁻¹ east while a wind blows it 75 m·s⁻¹ north. What is its resultant ground speed?
A 50 N weight rests on a slope inclined at 30°. What is the component of the weight along the slope? (sin30° = 0.5)
items.explanation: Component along the slope = mg sinθ = 50 × sin30° = 50 × 0.5 = 25 N.

items.question: A 50 N weight rests on a slope inclined at 30°. What is the component of the weight perpendicular to the slope? (cos30° = 0.866)
items.explanation: Component perpendicular = mg cosθ = 50 × cos30° = 50 × 0.866 = 43.3 N.

items.question: When resolving a vector F at angle θ to the horizontal, which pair of components is correct?
items.explanation: Measured from the horizontal, the horizontal component is Fcosθ and the vertical is Fsinθ.

L10.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply the gas laws (Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac) and the general gas equation

items.question: What does Boyle's Law state (at constant temperature)?
items.expectedAnswer: Pressure and volume are inversely proportional (pV = constant).
items.explanation: Boyle: at constant T, pV is constant (p up ⇒ V down).
options: Pressure and volume are inversely proportional (pV = constant).
Pressure and volume are directly proportional.
Volume and temperature are inversely proportional.

items.question: What does Charles' Law state (at constant pressure)?
items.expectedAnswer: Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (V/T = constant).
items.explanation: Charles: at constant p, V/T is constant (in kelvin).
options: Volume is inversely proportional to temperature.
Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (V/T = constant).

items.question: Before using any gas law, temperature must be converted to...
items.explanation: Gas-law temperatures are always in kelvin: K = °C + 273.

items.question: Convert 27 °C to kelvin.
What does Gay-Lussac's (pressure) law state (at constant volume)?
items.expectedAnswer: Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature (p/T = constant).
items.explanation: At constant volume, p/T is constant (in kelvin).
options: Pressure is inversely proportional to temperature.
Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature (p/T = constant).

items.question: Which equation is the general (combined) gas equation?
items.explanation: The combined gas law: p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂ (T in kelvin).

items.question: At constant temperature, if the volume of a gas is halved, the pressure...
items.explanation: Boyle's Law: p and V are inversely proportional, so halving V doubles p.

items.question: A gas at constant pressure is heated. Its volume will...
items.explanation: Charles' Law: higher temperature gives a larger volume at constant pressure.

items.question: A gas has volume 2 dm³ at 100 kPa. At constant temperature, what is its volume at 200 kPa?
items.explanation: Boyle: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ ⇒ 100 × 2 = 200 × V₂ ⇒ V₂ = 1 dm³.

items.question: Convert 127 °C to kelvin.
A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 300 K. At constant pressure, what volume does it occupy at 400 K?
items.explanation: Charles: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ ⇒ 300/300 = V₂/400 ⇒ V₂ = 400 cm³.

items.question: A gas at 100 kPa and 200 K is heated at constant volume to 400 K. What is the new pressure?
items.explanation: Gay-Lussac: p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂ ⇒ 100/200 = p₂/400 ⇒ p₂ = 200 kPa.

items.question: A gas has p₁ = 120 kPa, V₁ = 2 dm³, T₁ = 300 K. After change V₂ = 4 dm³ and T₂ = 400 K. What is p₂?
Why must Celsius be converted to kelvin in Charles' Law?
items.expectedAnswer: Volume is proportional to ABSOLUTE temperature; Celsius can be zero or negative, breaking the ratio.
items.explanation: The proportionality holds only on the absolute (kelvin) scale, where temperature cannot be negative.
options: Kelvin and Celsius give the same answer.
Volume is proportional to ABSOLUTE temperature; Celsius can be zero or negative, breaking the ratio.

items.question: A balloon has volume 1.5 dm³ at 27 °C. At constant pressure, what is its volume at 87 °C?
A gas at 200 kPa is compressed at constant temperature from 6 dm³ to 2 dm³. What is the new pressure?
items.explanation: Boyle: p₂ = p₁V₁/V₂ = 200 × 6/2 = 600 kPa.

items.question: On a graph of pressure vs volume (at constant T), Boyle's Law gives what shape?
items.explanation: Inverse proportionality (pV = constant) gives a curved graph, not a straight line.
options: A straight line through the origin.

items.question: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. Which gas law applies (volume fixed)?
items.explanation: With fixed volume, pressure rises with temperature — Gay-Lussac's law.

items.question: A gas at 400 K and 2 dm³ is cooled to 200 K at constant pressure. What is the new volume?
items.explanation: Charles: V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁ = 2 × 200/400 = 1 dm³.

items.question: Why does a sealed can of gas risk bursting when thrown into a fire?
items.expectedAnswer: The temperature rises at constant volume, so the pressure rises sharply (Gay-Lussac).
items.explanation: At fixed volume, heating raises the pressure (p/T constant), which can rupture the can.
options: The gas volume increases inside the rigid can.
The temperature rises at constant volume, so the pressure rises sharply (Gay-Lussac).
The pressure drops as it heats.

L10.T1.A2.skill_title: Apply the ideal gas equation and kinetic theory of gases

items.question: Which equation is the ideal gas equation?
items.explanation: The ideal gas equation: pV = nRT (R is the universal gas constant).

items.question: In pV = nRT, what does n represent?
items.expectedAnswer: The number of moles of gas.
items.explanation: n is the amount of gas in moles.
options: The number of moles of gas.
The mass of the gas in grams.

items.question: In the ideal gas equation, temperature T must be in...
items.explanation: T must always be in kelvin in pV = nRT.

items.question: Which is an assumption of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
items.expectedAnswer: Gas particles have negligible volume and no forces between them.
items.explanation: Ideal gas particles are treated as point masses with no intermolecular forces, in constant motion.
options: Gas particles have negligible volume and no forces between them.
Gas particles attract each other strongly.

items.question: According to kinetic theory, the collisions between ideal gas particles are...
items.explanation: Ideal gas collisions are perfectly elastic — total kinetic energy is conserved.

items.question: Real gases behave MOST like ideal gases at...
items.explanation: At high T and low p, particles are far apart and fast, so forces and volume are negligible (most ideal).

items.question: What causes the pressure of a gas in a container?
items.expectedAnswer: Gas particles colliding with the container walls.
items.explanation: Pressure arises from the force of countless particle collisions with the walls.
options: Gas particles colliding with the container walls.

items.question: The average kinetic energy of gas particles depends on the gas's...
items.explanation: Average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute (kelvin) temperature.

items.question: When using pV = nRT with SI units, pressure should be in...
items.explanation: In SI units pressure is in pascals, volume in m³, with R = 8.31 J·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹.

items.question: Heating a gas (at fixed volume) makes its particles move...
items.explanation: Higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy, so particles move faster.

items.question: How many moles of an ideal gas occupy 0.0249 m³ at 100 000 Pa and 300 K? (R = 8.31 J·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹)
A gas occupies 0.05 m³ at 200 000 Pa and 400 K. How many moles are present? (R = 8.31)
Why do real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure?
items.expectedAnswer: Particles are forced close together, so their volume and attractions are no longer negligible.
items.explanation: At high pressure the particles' own volume and intermolecular forces become significant, so real gases deviate.
options: Particles are forced close together, so their volume and attractions are no longer negligible.
The particles move faster than light.
Pressure has no effect on gases.

items.question: 2 moles of an ideal gas are at 300 K in a 0.05 m³ container. What is the pressure? (R = 8.31)
At the same temperature, which gas particles move faster on average: lighter or heavier ones?
items.expectedAnswer: Lighter particles (same average KE, smaller mass ⇒ higher speed).
items.explanation: At equal temperature the average KE is equal; lighter particles must move faster to have the same ½mv².
options: They move at the same speed.
Lighter particles (same average KE, smaller mass ⇒ higher speed).

items.question: What happens to gas pressure (fixed volume and amount) if the absolute temperature doubles?
items.explanation: From pV = nRT at fixed V and n, p ∝ T, so doubling T doubles p.

items.question: Why is the kinetic energy of gas particles said to be zero only at absolute zero (0 K)?
items.expectedAnswer: At 0 K particle motion theoretically stops, so kinetic energy is zero.
items.explanation: Absolute zero is the temperature at which particle motion (and kinetic energy) would theoretically cease.
options: At 0 K particle motion theoretically stops, so kinetic energy is zero.

items.question: A 0.5 mol sample of gas is at 250 000 Pa in 0.004 m³. What is its temperature? (R = 8.31)
Doubling the number of moles of gas (fixed T and V) does what to the pressure?
items.explanation: From pV = nRT at fixed T and V, p ∝ n, so doubling the moles doubles the pressure.

items.question: Which statement about an ideal gas is FALSE?
items.expectedAnswer: Its particles strongly attract each other.
items.explanation: Ideal gas particles are assumed to have NO intermolecular forces — the 'strong attraction' statement is false.
options: Its particles are in constant random motion.
Its particles strongly attract each other.

L11.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply moles, molar volume and concentration in calculations

items.question: Which equation relates moles (n), mass (m) and molar mass (M)?
items.explanation: n = m/M (mass ÷ molar mass).

items.question: Which equation gives concentration?
items.explanation: Concentration = moles ÷ volume (dm³): c = n/V.

items.question: What volume does 1 mole of gas occupy at STP?
items.explanation: At STP, 1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm³.

items.question: How many moles are in 49 g of H₂SO₄? (M = 98 g·mol⁻¹)
What is the concentration of 0.5 mol of NaCl dissolved in 2 dm³ of solution?
How do you convert cm³ to dm³?
items.explanation: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so divide cm³ by 1000.

items.question: How many moles of gas are in 11.2 dm³ at STP?
What is the mass of 2 mol of CaCO₃? (M = 100 g·mol⁻¹)
How many moles of solute are in 0.5 dm³ of a 2 mol·dm⁻³ solution?
What is the molar mass of NaOH? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
How many moles are in 250 cm³ of a 0.4 mol·dm⁻³ solution?
What mass of NaCl is needed to make 500 cm³ of a 1 mol·dm⁻³ solution? (M = 58.5 g·mol⁻¹)
What volume (at STP) is occupied by 4 g of helium gas? (He = 4 g·mol⁻¹)
What is the concentration when 9.8 g of H₂SO₄ is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution? (M = 98 g·mol⁻¹)
How many moles of CO₂ are in 5.6 dm³ at STP?
How many molecules are in 0.5 mol of a gas? (Nₐ = 6.02×10²³)
items.explanation: N = n × Nₐ = 0.5 × 6.02×10²³ = 3.01×10²³ molecules.

items.question: What mass of oxygen gas (O₂, M = 32 g·mol⁻¹) occupies 11.2 dm³ at STP?
A 0.2 mol·dm⁻³ solution has a volume of 750 cm³. How many moles of solute does it contain?
What is the concentration of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH (M = 40) in 200 cm³?
How many moles of nitrogen gas are in 44.8 dm³ at STP?

L11.T1.A2.skill_title: Solve limiting reagent, percentage yield, percentage purity and empirical formula problems

items.question: What is the limiting reagent in a reaction?
items.expectedAnswer: The reactant that runs out first and limits the amount of product.
items.explanation: The limiting reagent is fully used up first, setting the maximum amount of product.
options: The reactant that runs out first and limits the amount of product.
The reactant present in the largest amount.
The reactant with the highest molar mass.

items.question: Which equation gives percentage yield?
items.explanation: % yield = (actual/theoretical) × 100.

items.question: Which equation gives percentage purity?
items.expectedAnswer: (mass of pure substance ÷ mass of sample) × 100
items.explanation: % purity = (pure mass/total sample mass) × 100.
options: (mass of pure substance ÷ mass of sample) × 100

items.question: What is an empirical formula?
items.expectedAnswer: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
items.explanation: The empirical formula is the simplest ratio (e.g. CH₂O), which may differ from the molecular formula.
options: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
The actual number of atoms in a molecule.

items.question: To find an empirical formula, after converting masses to moles you...
items.expectedAnswer: divide each by the smallest number of moles.
items.explanation: Divide each mole value by the smallest to get the simplest whole-number ratio.
options: divide each by the smallest number of moles.

items.question: A reaction's theoretical yield is 50 g but only 40 g is obtained. What is the percentage yield?
A 20 g sample of limestone contains 16 g of pure CaCO₃. What is its percentage purity?
What is 'water of crystallisation'?
items.expectedAnswer: Water molecules that are part of a crystal's structure (a hydrate).
items.explanation: Water of crystallisation is built into the crystal lattice of a hydrated salt (e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O).
options: Water used to dissolve a salt.
Water molecules that are part of a crystal's structure (a hydrate).

items.question: Why is the actual yield usually less than the theoretical yield?
items.expectedAnswer: Reactions may be incomplete or product is lost during the process.
items.explanation: Side reactions, incomplete reactions and losses mean the actual yield is typically below the theoretical maximum.
options: The theoretical yield is always wrong.
Reactions may be incomplete or product is lost during the process.

items.question: A compound contains 1 mol of carbon and 2 mol of hydrogen and 1 mol of oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
items.explanation: The simplest ratio C:H:O = 1:2:1 gives CH₂O.

items.question: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, you have 2 mol N₂ and 3 mol H₂. Which is the limiting reagent?
items.explanation: 3 mol H₂ needs 1 mol N₂; you have plenty of N₂ (2 mol) but H₂ runs out first, so H₂ is limiting.

items.question: A compound is 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (C=12, H=1, O=16)
8 g of methane (CH₄, M=16) reacts with excess oxygen. The theoretical yield of CO₂ is 0.5 mol. If 0.4 mol forms, what is the percentage yield?
A 50 g impure sample contains 35 g of pure NaCl. What is its percentage purity?
In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, you have 4 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂. Which reactant is limiting?
items.explanation: 4 mol H₂ needs 2 mol O₂, but only 1 mol O₂ is present, so O₂ runs out first — it is limiting.

items.question: A hydrate has 1 mol of MgSO₄ to 7 mol of H₂O. What is its formula?
items.explanation: The ratio of salt to water (1:7) gives MgSO₄·7H₂O.

items.question: Why must you identify the limiting reagent before calculating product amounts?
items.expectedAnswer: Because the limiting reagent determines how much product can form.
items.explanation: Product is limited by the reactant that runs out first, so calculations must be based on it.
options: Because the excess reagent decides the product.
Because the limiting reagent determines how much product can form.

items.question: A compound has empirical formula CH₂ and molar mass 42 g·mol⁻¹. What is its molecular formula? (CH₂ = 14)
items.explanation: 42/14 = 3, so the molecular formula is (CH₂)₃ = C₃H₆.

items.question: 10 g of CaCO₃ (M=100) is heated and produces 0.08 mol of CO₂. The theoretical yield is 0.1 mol. What is the percentage yield?
A 4 g sample of impure zinc reacts; only 3.2 g is pure zinc. What is the percentage purity?

L12.T1.A1.skill_title: Classify reactions as exothermic/endothermic and interpret potential-energy diagrams

items.question: What is an exothermic reaction?
items.expectedAnswer: One that releases energy to the surroundings.
items.explanation: Exothermic reactions release energy (the surroundings get warmer).
options: One that releases energy to the surroundings.
One that absorbs energy from the surroundings.

items.question: What is an endothermic reaction?
items.expectedAnswer: One that absorbs energy from the surroundings.
items.explanation: Endothermic reactions absorb energy (the surroundings get colder).
options: One that absorbs energy from the surroundings.

items.question: For an exothermic reaction, the sign of ΔH (heat of reaction) is...
items.explanation: Exothermic releases energy, so ΔH is negative.

items.question: For an endothermic reaction, the sign of ΔH is...
items.explanation: Endothermic absorbs energy, so ΔH is positive.

items.question: Breaking chemical bonds...
items.explanation: Bond breaking requires (absorbs) energy.

items.question: Forming chemical bonds...
items.explanation: Bond forming releases energy.

items.question: On a potential-energy diagram, what is the activated complex?
items.expectedAnswer: The high-energy, unstable arrangement at the peak of the curve.
items.explanation: The activated complex is the unstable species at the maximum (peak) of the energy profile.
options: The high-energy, unstable arrangement at the peak of the curve.

items.question: On a potential-energy diagram, what does the activation energy represent?
items.expectedAnswer: The energy from the reactants up to the peak.
items.explanation: Activation energy is the energy needed to reach the activated complex (reactants → peak).
options: The energy difference between reactants and products.
The energy from the reactants up to the peak.
The total energy of the products.

items.question: In an exothermic reaction, the products are... than the reactants on a potential-energy diagram.
items.explanation: Exothermic releases energy, so the products sit lower than the reactants.

items.question: In an endothermic reaction, the products are... than the reactants on a potential-energy diagram.
items.explanation: Endothermic absorbs energy, so the products sit higher than the reactants.

items.question: A reaction's potential-energy diagram shows products LOWER than reactants. What can you conclude?
items.explanation: Products lower than reactants means energy was released — exothermic, ΔH negative.

items.question: If the energy released in forming bonds is GREATER than the energy absorbed in breaking bonds, the reaction is...
items.explanation: Net energy released (more out than in) makes the reaction exothermic.

items.question: How does a catalyst affect the activation energy and ΔH of a reaction?
items.expectedAnswer: It lowers the activation energy but does not change ΔH.
items.explanation: A catalyst provides a lower-energy pathway (lower Ea) but the overall energy change ΔH is unchanged.
options: It lowers the activation energy but does not change ΔH.
It lowers both activation energy and ΔH.

items.question: Reactants have a potential energy of 150 kJ and products 90 kJ. What is ΔH?
items.explanation: ΔH = products − reactants = 90 − 150 = −60 kJ (exothermic).

items.question: Reactants have a potential energy of 80 kJ and products 130 kJ. What is ΔH?
items.explanation: ΔH = 130 − 80 = +50 kJ (endothermic).

items.question: Why does a reaction need activation energy even if it is exothermic overall?
items.expectedAnswer: Bonds must first be broken (energy in) before new bonds form (energy out).
items.explanation: Even exothermic reactions need an initial energy input to reach the activated complex.
options: Bonds must first be broken (energy in) before new bonds form (energy out).
Exothermic reactions need no activation energy.

items.question: Which everyday process is endothermic?
items.explanation: Photosynthesis absorbs energy (light), making it endothermic; combustion and respiration release energy.

items.question: The activation energy for the forward reaction is 70 kJ and ΔH is −30 kJ. What is the activation energy for the reverse reaction?
items.explanation: Reverse Ea = forward Ea − ΔH = 70 − (−30) = 100 kJ.

items.question: On a potential-energy diagram, the heat of reaction (ΔH) is measured as the energy difference between...
items.explanation: ΔH is the energy gap between reactants and products (not involving the peak).
options: the reactants and the activated complex.
the products and the activated complex.

items.question: A reaction mixture becomes warmer as it proceeds. The bonds formed in the products must have released...
items.expectedAnswer: more energy than was needed to break the reactant bonds.
items.explanation: A temperature rise (exothermic) means bond formation released more energy than bond breaking absorbed.
options: less energy than was needed to break the reactant bonds.
more energy than was needed to break the reactant bonds.

L13.T1.A1.skill_title: Predict the products of acid reactions and neutralisation

items.question: What are the products of acid + metal?
items.explanation: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas.

items.question: What are the products of an acid-base neutralisation (acid + metal hydroxide)?
items.explanation: Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water (neutralisation).

items.question: What are the products of acid + metal carbonate?
items.explanation: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂.

items.question: Which gas is released when a metal reacts with an acid?
items.explanation: Acid + metal produces hydrogen gas (often seen as bubbles, gives a 'pop' test).

items.question: Which acid produces chloride salts?
items.explanation: HCl gives chloride salts; H₂SO₄ gives sulfates; HNO₃ gives nitrates.

items.question: Which acid produces sulfate salts?
items.explanation: H₂SO₄ produces sulfate salts (SO₄²⁻).

items.question: What salt forms when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
items.explanation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O; the salt is sodium chloride.

items.question: When an acid reacts with a metal oxide, the products are...
items.explanation: Acid + metal oxide → salt + water (a neutralisation).

items.question: What observation indicates an acid + carbonate reaction?
items.explanation: Acid + carbonate releases CO₂, seen as fizzing/effervescence.

items.question: A neutralisation reaction always produces which substance?
items.explanation: Neutralisation (acid + base) always produces water (and a salt).

items.question: What salt forms when sulfuric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide?
items.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O; the salt is potassium sulfate.

items.question: Complete: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + ?
items.explanation: Acid + metal gives a salt plus hydrogen gas: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

items.question: Complete: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + ?
items.explanation: Acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.

items.question: Which balanced equation correctly shows the neutralisation of HCl by NaOH?
items.explanation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is balanced (1:1, salt + water).

items.question: What salt forms when nitric acid reacts with sodium carbonate?
items.explanation: HNO₃ gives nitrate salts: 2HNO₃ + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

items.question: Why is the reaction of an acid with a metal NOT classed as a neutralisation?
items.expectedAnswer: It produces hydrogen gas, not just water with a salt.
items.explanation: Neutralisation gives salt + water; acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen, so it is different.
options: It produces hydrogen gas, not just water with a salt.
It does not involve an acid.

items.question: Balance: H₂SO₄ + NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O. How many NaOH are needed?
items.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (two NaOH balance the two sodiums and hydrogens).

items.question: A metal oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid. Predict the products of CuO + 2HCl.
items.explanation: Acid + metal oxide → salt + water: CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O.

items.question: Which reaction would produce a gas that relights a glowing splint? (Hint: that gas is oxygen — which of these does NOT make it?)
items.expectedAnswer: None of these acid reactions make oxygen.
items.explanation: Acid + metal makes hydrogen; acid + carbonate makes CO₂. Neither makes oxygen, so none relights a glowing splint.
options: None of these acid reactions make oxygen.

items.question: Zinc reacts with sulfuric acid. What are the products?
items.explanation: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ (acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; H₂SO₄ gives a sulfate).

L14.T1.A1.skill_title: Assign oxidation numbers and identify oxidation, reduction and agents

items.question: What is the oxidation number of an atom in its free (uncombined) element, e.g. O₂ or Cu?
items.explanation: Any element in its free (uncombined) state has an oxidation number of 0.

items.question: What is the usual oxidation number of oxygen in a compound?
items.explanation: Oxygen is usually −2 (except in peroxides, where it is −1).

items.question: What is the usual oxidation number of hydrogen in a compound?
items.explanation: Hydrogen is usually +1 (except in metal hydrides, where it is −1).

items.question: What does oxidation mean in terms of oxidation number?
items.expectedAnswer: An increase in oxidation number (loss of electrons).
items.explanation: Oxidation = increase in oxidation number = loss of electrons.
options: An increase in oxidation number (loss of electrons).

items.question: What does reduction mean in terms of oxidation number?
items.expectedAnswer: A decrease in oxidation number (gain of electrons).
items.explanation: Reduction = decrease in oxidation number = gain of electrons.
options: A decrease in oxidation number (gain of electrons).

items.question: In a neutral compound, the sum of all oxidation numbers must equal...
items.explanation: Oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule sum to zero.

items.question: In a polyatomic ion, the sum of the oxidation numbers equals...
items.explanation: For an ion, the oxidation numbers sum to the ion's overall charge.

items.question: What is the oxidation number of sodium in NaCl?
items.explanation: Group 1 metals are always +1, so Na is +1 (and Cl is −1).

items.question: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in NaCl?
items.explanation: Na is +1, so Cl must be −1 for the sum to be zero.

items.question: An oxidising agent is the substance that...
items.explanation: An oxidising agent oxidises something else, so it is itself reduced (gains electrons).

items.question: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in SO₄²⁻?
items.explanation: Four O at −2 = −8; for the ion's −2 charge, S must be +6 (since +6 − 8 = −2).

items.question: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in NO₃⁻?
items.explanation: Three O at −2 = −6; for the −1 charge, N = +5 (since +5 − 6 = −1).

items.question: What is the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₄⁻?
items.explanation: Four O at −2 = −8; for the −1 charge, Mn = +7 (since +7 − 8 = −1).

items.question: What is the oxidation number of carbon in CO₂?
items.explanation: Two O at −2 = −4; for a neutral molecule, C = +4.

items.question: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂?
items.explanation: Peroxides are an exception: oxygen is −1 in H₂O₂ (two H at +1 balance two O at −1).

items.question: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species is oxidised?
items.explanation: Zinc's oxidation number rises from 0 to +2, so it is oxidised (loses electrons).

items.question: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species is the oxidising agent?
items.explanation: Cu²⁺ gains electrons (reduced from +2 to 0), so it is the oxidising agent.

items.question: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what happens to the oxygen?
items.explanation: Oxygen goes from 0 in O₂ to −2 in MgO — a decrease, so it is reduced.

items.question: How can you tell a reaction is NOT a redox reaction?
items.explanation: If no atom's oxidation number changes, no electrons are transferred, so it is not redox.

items.question: In the reaction Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺, the iron is...
items.explanation: The oxidation number drops from +3 to +2 as it gains an electron — reduction.

L15.T1.A1.skill_title: Describe mining, mineral extraction and its impact in the lithosphere

items.question: What is the lithosphere?
items.expectedAnswer: The solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth.
items.explanation: The lithosphere is Earth's solid rocky outer shell, rich in minerals.
options: The solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth.
The layer of air around the Earth.

items.question: What is an ore?
items.expectedAnswer: A rock or mineral from which a metal can be profitably extracted.
items.explanation: An ore is a naturally occurring material containing enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting.
options: A pure metal found in the ground.
A rock or mineral from which a metal can be profitably extracted.

items.question: Most metals are found in the Earth as...
items.expectedAnswer: compounds in ores, not as pure elements.
items.explanation: Reactive metals occur as compounds (ores) and must be chemically extracted.
options: compounds in ores, not as pure elements.

items.question: Why is energy needed to extract a metal from its ore?
items.expectedAnswer: Chemical reactions (e.g. reduction or electrolysis) are required to free the metal.
items.explanation: Breaking the metal-compound bonds (by reduction or electrolysis) requires energy.
options: Chemical reactions (e.g. reduction or electrolysis) are required to free the metal.
Metals are simply picked up as pure elements.

items.question: Which is a major mineral resource that South Africa is well known for mining?
items.explanation: South Africa is a major producer of gold, platinum and other minerals.

items.question: Which is an environmental impact of mining?
items.expectedAnswer: Pollution of water, air and land.
items.explanation: Mining can pollute water (acid mine drainage), air (dust) and damage land.
options: Pollution of water, air and land.

items.question: Why should mineral resources be used responsibly?
items.expectedAnswer: They are limited (non-renewable) and mining has social and environmental costs.
items.explanation: Minerals are finite and mining carries costs, so responsible, sustainable use is important.
options: They are limited (non-renewable) and mining has social and environmental costs.

items.question: A reactive metal like aluminium is usually extracted by...
items.explanation: Very reactive metals (e.g. aluminium) are extracted by electrolysis.

items.question: What is 'acid mine drainage'?
items.expectedAnswer: Acidic, metal-rich water that flows from mines and pollutes the environment.
items.explanation: Acid mine drainage is polluted acidic water from mining that harms rivers and groundwater.
options: Acidic, metal-rich water that flows from mines and pollutes the environment.

items.question: Mining benefits society mainly by...
items.expectedAnswer: providing materials, jobs and economic income.
items.explanation: Mining provides raw materials, employment and economic benefits, alongside its costs.
options: providing materials, jobs and economic income.

items.question: Iron is extracted from its ore (e.g. Fe₂O₃) by...
items.expectedAnswer: reduction (removing oxygen, e.g. with carbon in a blast furnace).
items.explanation: Iron is extracted by reduction of iron oxide (removing oxygen) using carbon/carbon monoxide.
options: reduction (removing oxygen, e.g. with carbon in a blast furnace).

items.question: Why does extracting a metal by electrolysis use a lot of energy?
items.expectedAnswer: Electrical energy is needed to break the strong bonds in the molten ore.
items.explanation: Electrolysis drives a non-spontaneous reaction, requiring large amounts of electrical energy.
options: Electrical energy is needed to break the strong bonds in the molten ore.

items.question: Why is recycling metals beneficial for the lithosphere?
items.expectedAnswer: It reduces the need for mining and conserves limited ore resources.
items.explanation: Recycling reuses metals, lowering demand for mining and conserving finite ore reserves.
options: It reduces the need for mining and conserves limited ore resources.
It creates new ore in the ground.

items.question: A mine pollutes a nearby river with acidic water and dissolved metals. This is an example of...
items.expectedAnswer: a negative environmental impact of mining.
items.explanation: Polluting water with acid and metals is a negative environmental impact (acid mine drainage).
options: a negative environmental impact of mining.
a way to purify the river.

items.question: Why must a balance be found between mining and conservation?
items.expectedAnswer: Mining brings economic benefit but harms the environment, which must be protected for the future.
items.explanation: Sustainable use balances the economic value of mining against protecting the environment.
options: Mining brings economic benefit but harms the environment, which must be protected for the future.

items.question: Why can gold sometimes be found as the native (pure) metal, unlike iron?
items.expectedAnswer: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not readily form compounds.
items.explanation: Gold's low reactivity means it often occurs as the uncombined metal, unlike reactive iron.
options: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not readily form compounds.
Gold is the most reactive metal.

items.question: Dust released during mining and crushing of rock mainly affects which system?
items.explanation: Mining dust pollutes the air, affecting the atmosphere and human health.

items.question: The method used to extract a metal depends mainly on...
items.explanation: Reactive metals need electrolysis; less reactive ones can be reduced with carbon — reactivity decides the method.
options: the depth of the mine only.

items.question: Why are mineral resources described as non-renewable?
items.expectedAnswer: They form over millions of years and cannot be replaced on a human timescale.
items.explanation: Ores take geological ages to form, so once mined they are effectively non-renewable.
options: They form over millions of years and cannot be replaced on a human timescale.

items.question: Rehabilitating land after mining is important because it...
items.expectedAnswer: restores the environment damaged by mining.
items.explanation: Rehabilitation repairs mined land, reducing long-term environmental harm.
options: restores the environment damaged by mining.

L2.T1.A1.skill_title: State Newton's laws, draw free-body diagrams and apply Fnet = ma to a single body

items.question: What does Newton's First Law state?
items.expectedAnswer: A body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a non-zero net force.
items.explanation: Newton's First Law (inertia): no net force means no change in motion.
options: A body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a non-zero net force.
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

items.question: What does Newton's Second Law state?
items.expectedAnswer: The net force equals mass times acceleration (Fnet = ma).
items.explanation: Newton's Second Law: Fnet = ma, acceleration in the direction of the net force.
options: A body at rest stays at rest.
The net force equals mass times acceleration (Fnet = ma).

items.question: What does Newton's Third Law state?
items.expectedAnswer: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force on a different body.
items.explanation: Newton's Third Law: action–reaction pairs are equal, opposite, and act on different objects.
options: A body keeps moving at constant velocity.
Net force equals mass times acceleration.
For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force on a different body.

items.question: A free-body diagram shows...
items.expectedAnswer: all the forces acting ON one chosen object.
items.explanation: A free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on the single chosen body.
options: all the forces acting ON one chosen object.
the forces the object exerts on other things.
the velocity and position of the object.

items.question: A 5 kg object experiences a net force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
items.explanation: Fnet = ma ⇒ a = Fnet/m = 10/5 = 2 m·s⁻².

items.question: What is the weight of a 4 kg object? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
items.explanation: Weight = mg = 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N.

items.question: An object moves at constant velocity. What is the net force on it?
items.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Fnet = ma the net force is zero.

items.question: Which is an example of a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.expectedAnswer: A swimmer pushes water back; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
items.explanation: Action–reaction pairs act on different bodies: swimmer on water, water on swimmer.
options: The weight of a book and the normal force on it.
A swimmer pushes water back; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
Friction and the applied force on a box.

items.question: A 2 kg trolley accelerates at 3 m·s⁻². What net force acts on it?
items.explanation: Fnet = ma = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

items.question: Why is the weight and the normal force on a book on a table NOT a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.expectedAnswer: They act on the same body (the book), not on two different bodies.
items.explanation: Third Law pairs act on different objects; weight and normal force both act on the book.
options: They act on the same body (the book), not on two different bodies.
They are not equal in size.
They act in the same direction.

items.question: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 2.5 m·s⁻². What net force is needed?
A 10 kg box is pushed with 50 N forward while 20 N of friction opposes it. What is its acceleration?
A 3 kg object on a frictionless floor is pulled with a horizontal force of 12 N. What is its acceleration?
items.explanation: No friction, so Fnet = 12 N; a = 12/3 = 4 m·s⁻².

items.question: A 6 kg object is lifted by a rope with a tension of 70 N. What is its acceleration? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
Why does a passenger lurch forward when a bus suddenly brakes?
items.expectedAnswer: Inertia — the passenger tends to keep moving (Newton's First Law).
items.explanation: By inertia (First Law), the body keeps moving forward when the bus decelerates.
options: Inertia — the passenger tends to keep moving (Newton's First Law).

items.question: A net force of 24 N gives an object an acceleration of 6 m·s⁻². What is the object's mass?
items.explanation: Fnet = ma ⇒ m = Fnet/a = 24/6 = 4 kg.

items.question: On the free-body diagram of a box resting on the floor, which forces act?
items.explanation: Forces ON the box: its weight down and the normal force up; the box's push on the floor is not on the box.
options: Normal force and the force of the box on the floor.

items.question: A 0.5 kg ball in free fall (ignoring air resistance) has what net force on it? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
items.explanation: The only force is weight: Fnet = mg = 0.5 × 9.8 = 4.9 N downward.

items.question: A 4 kg object is pushed with 30 N but does not move. What is the friction force on it?
items.explanation: Not moving ⇒ zero acceleration ⇒ net force zero, so static friction balances the push: 30 N.

items.question: Two forces act on a 5 kg object: 40 N right and 15 N left. What is its acceleration?
items.explanation: Fnet = 40 − 15 = 25 N right; a = 25/5 = 5 m·s⁻².

L2.T1.A2.skill_title: Apply Newton's laws to connected bodies, inclined planes and friction

items.question: On a frictionless inclined plane, what is the component of weight acting DOWN the slope?
items.explanation: The down-slope component of weight is mg sinθ (θ measured from the horizontal).

items.question: On an inclined plane, what is the component of weight PERPENDICULAR to the slope?
items.explanation: The perpendicular component (equal to the normal force) is mg cosθ.

items.question: Which equation gives the friction force?
items.explanation: Friction force = coefficient of friction × normal force: f = μN.

items.question: What does the normal force equal for an object on a horizontal surface (no vertical applied force)?
items.explanation: On a flat surface with no extra vertical force, the normal force balances the weight: N = mg.

items.question: Kinetic friction acts when an object is...
items.explanation: Kinetic (sliding) friction acts while an object moves; static friction acts before it slides.

items.question: A 4 kg block on a horizontal surface has μ = 0.3. What is the kinetic friction force? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
In connected bodies joined by a single inextensible string, the tension is...
items.explanation: A single light inextensible string has the same tension throughout.

items.question: Two blocks (2 kg and 3 kg) are connected and pulled together. To find their shared acceleration, treat them as...
items.expectedAnswer: a single system of total mass 5 kg.
items.explanation: For shared acceleration, treat connected bodies as one combined mass (2 + 3 = 5 kg).
options: a single system of total mass 5 kg.

items.question: A 10 N down-slope force acts on a block held still on a slope. What is the static friction force?
items.explanation: If the block is stationary, static friction balances the down-slope force: 10 N up the slope.

items.question: Why does increasing the angle of an incline increase the tendency of a block to slide?
items.expectedAnswer: The down-slope component mg sinθ increases with θ.
items.explanation: As θ rises, mg sinθ (down-slope force) increases while mg cosθ (and friction) decreases, so it slides more easily.
options: The down-slope component mg sinθ increases with θ.
The normal force increases with θ.

items.question: A 5 kg block on a 30° frictionless incline. What is its acceleration down the slope? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻², sin30° = 0.5)
items.explanation: a = g sinθ = 9.8 × 0.5 = 4.9 m·s⁻² (mass cancels on a frictionless incline).

items.question: A 2 kg and a 3 kg block are connected by a string and pulled by 20 N on a frictionless surface. What is their acceleration?
items.explanation: Treat as one system: a = F/(m₁+m₂) = 20/(2+3) = 4 m·s⁻².

items.question: For the 2 kg and 3 kg connected blocks above (a = 4 m·s⁻², 20 N pulling the 3 kg block), what is the tension in the string pulling the 2 kg block?
items.explanation: Isolate the 2 kg block: T = m₁a = 2 × 4 = 8 N.

items.question: A 6 kg block on a horizontal surface (μ = 0.2) is pushed with 30 N. What is its acceleration? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
A block on a 20° incline is on the verge of sliding. What does the coefficient of static friction equal? (tan20° = 0.364)
items.explanation: On the verge of sliding, μs = tanθ = tan20° = 0.364.

items.question: Why is the normal force on a slope LESS than the object's weight?
items.expectedAnswer: The normal force equals only mg cosθ, the perpendicular component.
items.explanation: On a slope the surface only supports the perpendicular component, N = mg cosθ < mg.
options: The normal force equals only mg cosθ, the perpendicular component.
The normal force equals mg sinθ.
The weight decreases on a slope.

items.question: A 4 kg block on a 30° incline with friction force 5 N. What is its acceleration down the slope? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻², sin30° = 0.5)
Two masses hang over a frictionless pulley: 3 kg and 5 kg (Atwood machine). What is the acceleration of the system? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
Why is static friction able to take a range of values up to a maximum?
items.expectedAnswer: It adjusts to balance the applied force until the object is on the verge of slipping.
items.explanation: Static friction matches the applied force up to f_max = μsN, then the object slips.
options: It adjusts to balance the applied force until the object is on the verge of slipping.
It is always at its maximum value.
It is always zero until movement begins.

items.question: A 2 kg block sits on top of a 3 kg block; the lower block is pulled so both accelerate together at 2 m·s⁻². What net force acts on the TOP block?
items.explanation: For the top block alone: Fnet = ma = 2 × 2 = 4 N (provided by friction from the lower block).

L2.T1.A3.skill_title: Apply Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

items.question: Which equation gives the gravitational force between two masses?
items.explanation: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation: F = GMm/r² (inverse square of distance).

items.question: In F = GMm/r², what does r represent?
items.expectedAnswer: The distance between the centres of the two masses.
items.explanation: r is the distance between the centres of the two masses.
options: The radius of only the smaller mass.
The distance between the centres of the two masses.

items.question: If the distance between two masses doubles, the gravitational force becomes...
items.expectedAnswer: one quarter of its original value.
items.explanation: Inverse-square law: doubling r divides F by 2² = 4.
options: one quarter of its original value.

items.question: What is the difference between mass and weight?
items.expectedAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter (constant); weight is the gravitational force (varies with g).
items.explanation: Mass is constant everywhere; weight = mg changes with the local gravitational field.
options: Mass is the amount of matter (constant); weight is the gravitational force (varies with g).
Weight is constant; mass changes with location.

items.question: Does an astronaut's mass change when they travel to the Moon?
items.expectedAnswer: No — mass stays the same; only weight changes.
items.explanation: Mass is constant; the smaller lunar g makes the astronaut weigh less, but their mass is unchanged.
options: Yes — mass decreases on the Moon.
No — mass stays the same; only weight changes.
Yes — mass increases on the Moon.

items.question: Which equation gives the gravitational acceleration g at a planet's surface?
items.explanation: g = GM/r², where M is the planet's mass and r its radius.

items.question: The gravitational force between two masses is always...
items.explanation: Gravitational force is always attractive between masses.

items.question: If one of the two masses is doubled, the gravitational force between them...
items.explanation: F is proportional to each mass, so doubling one mass doubles the force.

items.question: What is the weight of a 20 kg object on Earth? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²)
items.explanation: Weight = mg = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N.

items.question: Why do we usually ignore the gravitational force between two everyday objects (like two people)?
items.expectedAnswer: Their masses are too small to produce a noticeable force.
items.explanation: G is tiny, so for small everyday masses the gravitational force is negligible.
options: Their masses are too small to produce a noticeable force.
Gravity does not act on small objects.
G is zero for small objects.

items.question: If the distance between two masses is halved, the gravitational force becomes...
items.explanation: Inverse-square: halving r multiplies F by 1/(½)² = 4.

items.question: Both masses are doubled and the distance is kept the same. The gravitational force becomes...
items.explanation: F ∝ M × m, so doubling both multiplies F by 2 × 2 = 4.

items.question: A planet has the same mass as Earth but twice the radius. How does its surface g compare to Earth's?
items.expectedAnswer: It is one quarter of Earth's g.
items.explanation: g = GM/r²; same M but double r gives g/4 (inverse square of radius).
options: It is one quarter of Earth's g.
It is the same as Earth's g.

items.question: Calculate the force between a 1000 kg and a 2000 kg mass 2 m apart. (G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻²)
Why is your weight slightly less at the top of a high mountain than at sea level?
items.expectedAnswer: You are further from the Earth's centre, so g (and weight) is slightly smaller.
items.explanation: g = GM/r²; greater distance r from the centre means a smaller g and thus less weight (mass unchanged).
options: Gravity does not act at altitude.
You are further from the Earth's centre, so g (and weight) is slightly smaller.

items.question: A planet has twice Earth's mass and the same radius. How does its surface g compare to Earth's?
items.explanation: g = GM/r²; doubling M (same r) doubles g.

items.question: An object weighs 60 N on Earth (g = 9.8 m·s⁻²). What is its mass?
items.explanation: m = weight/g = 60/9.8 = 6.12 kg.

items.question: The Moon's gravitational acceleration is about 1.6 m·s⁻². What would a 10 kg object weigh on the Moon?
items.explanation: Weight = mg = 10 × 1.6 = 16 N (mass stays 10 kg).

items.question: Two masses exert a gravitational force F on each other. By Newton's Third Law, the force each exerts on the other is...
items.expectedAnswer: equal in size and opposite in direction.
items.explanation: Gravitational forces form a Third Law pair: equal and opposite on the two masses, regardless of their sizes.
options: equal in size and opposite in direction.

items.question: If both the distance is doubled AND one mass is doubled, the gravitational force becomes...
items.explanation: Doubling a mass ×2; doubling r ÷4. Net: 2/4 = ½ the original force.

items.question: What is refraction?
items.expectedAnswer: The bending of light as it changes speed crossing a boundary between media.
items.explanation: Refraction is the change in direction of light due to a change in speed at a boundary.
options: The bending of light as it changes speed crossing a boundary between media.
The bouncing of light off a surface.
The splitting of light into colours only.

items.question: From where is the angle of incidence measured?
items.expectedAnswer: From the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface).
items.explanation: Angles in optics are measured from the normal, not the surface.
options: From the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface).

items.question: How is refractive index defined?
items.expectedAnswer: n = c/v (speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in the medium).
items.explanation: Refractive index n = c/v; it is always ≥ 1.
options: n = c/v (speed of light in vacuum ÷ speed in the medium).

items.question: When light passes from air into glass (a denser medium), it bends...
items.explanation: Entering a denser (slower) medium, light bends towards the normal.

items.question: When light passes from glass into air (a less dense medium), it bends...
items.explanation: Entering a less dense (faster) medium, light bends away from the normal.

items.question: Which equation is Snell's Law?
items.explanation: Snell's Law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂.

items.question: A medium has a refractive index greater than 1. This means light travels...
items.expectedAnswer: slower in the medium than in a vacuum.
items.explanation: n = c/v > 1 means v < c, so light is slower in the medium.
options: slower in the medium than in a vacuum.
faster in the medium than in a vacuum.
at the same speed as in a vacuum.

items.question: Light in a vacuum has refractive index...
items.explanation: In a vacuum n = c/c = 1.

items.question: If light hits a boundary along the normal (angle of incidence 0°), what happens?
items.expectedAnswer: It passes straight through without bending.
items.explanation: At 0° incidence there is no bending; light continues straight (though its speed changes).
options: It passes straight through without bending.

items.question: The speed of light in glass is 2×10⁸ m·s⁻¹. What is the refractive index of the glass? (c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹)
Light travels from air (n = 1) into water (n = 1.33) at an angle of incidence of 30°. Find the angle of refraction. (sin30° = 0.5)
items.explanation: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ ⇒ sinθ₂ = (1 × 0.5)/1.33 = 0.376 ⇒ θ₂ = 22.1°.

items.question: Light goes from glass (n = 1.5) into air (n = 1) at an angle of incidence of 20°. Find the angle of refraction. (sin20° = 0.342)
items.explanation: sinθ₂ = (1.5 × 0.342)/1 = 0.513 ⇒ θ₂ = 30.9° (bends away from the normal).

items.question: Why does a straw in a glass of water appear bent at the surface?
items.expectedAnswer: Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water, changing direction.
items.explanation: Light bends (refracts) at the water-air boundary, making the submerged part appear displaced.
options: Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water, changing direction.
The straw physically bends in water.

items.question: A ray enters a medium and bends towards the normal. What can you conclude about the second medium?
items.expectedAnswer: It is denser (higher refractive index) than the first.
items.explanation: Bending towards the normal means entering a denser, slower medium (higher n).
options: It is less dense than the first.
It is denser (higher refractive index) than the first.
It has the same density as the first.

items.question: The refractive index of a diamond is 2.42. What is the speed of light in diamond? (c = 3×10⁸ m·s⁻¹)
Light travels from medium A (n = 1.2) to medium B (n = 1.6). Compared with medium A, the light in medium B is...
items.expectedAnswer: slower and bends towards the normal.
items.explanation: Higher n in B means slower light, bending towards the normal.
options: slower and bends towards the normal.
faster and bends away from the normal.

items.question: Light passes from water (n = 1.33) into air (n = 1.00) at 25° incidence. sin25° = 0.423. Find the angle of refraction.
Does the frequency of light change when it refracts into a new medium?
items.expectedAnswer: No — frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change.
items.explanation: On refraction frequency is unchanged; the speed and wavelength change together (v = fλ).
options: No — frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change.

items.question: A ray hits a glass surface and part of it changes direction on entering. The bending happens because...
items.expectedAnswer: the light changes speed at the boundary.
items.explanation: Refraction (bending) is caused by the change in light's speed crossing the boundary.
options: the light changes speed at the boundary.
the glass absorbs part of the light.

items.question: Two media have refractive indices 1.0 and 1.5. In which is the speed of light greater?
items.explanation: Lower n means higher speed (v = c/n), so light is faster where n = 1.0.
options: The speed is equal in both.

L3.T1.A2.skill_title: Apply the critical angle and total internal reflection

items.question: What is the critical angle?
items.expectedAnswer: The angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90°.
items.explanation: At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the surface (refraction angle = 90°).
options: The angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90°.
The angle at which light passes straight through.

items.question: What is total internal reflection?

Light passes straight through the boundary.

items.question: What is the FIRST condition for total internal reflection?
items.expectedAnswer: Light travels from a denser to a less dense medium.
items.explanation: TIR requires light moving from a denser (higher n) to a less dense (lower n) medium.
options: Light travels from a less dense to a denser medium.
Light hits the surface along the normal.
Light travels from a denser to a less dense medium.

items.question: What is the SECOND condition for total internal reflection?

items.explanation: The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle for TIR to occur.

The angle of incidence is less than the critical angle.
The angle of incidence is exactly zero.

items.question: Which equation gives the critical angle?

items.question: Optical fibres carry light signals using which effect?

items.question: At an angle of incidence exactly equal to the critical angle, the refracted ray...

items.question: Can total internal reflection occur when light goes from air into glass?

items.question: Below the critical angle (smaller angle of incidence), what happens to the light at the boundary?
items.expectedAnswer: Most of it refracts out of the medium.
items.explanation: Below θc the light refracts out (with some partial reflection); TIR only happens above θc.
options: Most of it refracts out of the medium.

items.question: Total internal reflection only happens at the boundary with a...
items.explanation: TIR occurs going into a less dense medium, where the critical angle exists.

items.question: A glass has refractive index 1.5 and is in air (n = 1). Find the critical angle. (sin⁻¹(0.667) = 41.8°)
Water has refractive index 1.33 (air = 1). Find the critical angle. (sin⁻¹(0.752) = 48.8°)

items.question: A light ray inside glass (θc = 42°) hits the glass-air surface at 30°. What happens?
items.expectedAnswer: It refracts out into the air (30° < 42°).
items.explanation: Below the critical angle (30° < 42°), the ray refracts out of the glass.
options: It refracts out into the air (30° < 42°).

items.question: A denser medium has a SMALLER critical angle than a less dense one. Why is this useful in optical fibres?
items.expectedAnswer: A small critical angle means more rays undergo total internal reflection, trapping the light.
items.explanation: A smaller θc means a wider range of angles cause TIR, keeping the signal inside the fibre.
options: A small critical angle lets light escape easily.
It has no effect on the fibre.
A small critical angle means more rays undergo total internal reflection, trapping the light.

items.question: Diamond has a very high refractive index (2.42) and so a small critical angle (~24°). How does this affect its sparkle?
items.expectedAnswer: Light is internally reflected many times before leaving, increasing the sparkle.
items.explanation: A small critical angle causes lots of total internal reflection, so light bounces around and exits brightly.
options: Light is internally reflected many times before leaving, increasing the sparkle.
Light passes straight through without reflecting.

items.question: A medium has critical angle 30° with air. What is its refractive index? (sin30° = 0.5)
Why does total internal reflection NOT occur when light goes from air into water?
items.expectedAnswer: There is no critical angle going from a less dense to a denser medium.
items.explanation: TIR requires denser → less dense; going less dense → denser, the ray always refracts in, so no TIR.
options: The critical angle is too large.
There is no critical angle going from a less dense to a denser medium.

items.question: An optical fibre's core must have a refractive index that is... compared with its cladding.
items.explanation: The core must be denser (higher n) so light travelling in it can totally internally reflect at the cladding.

items.question: At an angle of incidence just below the critical angle, the refracted ray is...
items.expectedAnswer: very close to 90° (nearly along the surface).

L4.T1.A1.skill_title: Describe wavefronts, Huygens' principle and diffraction

items.question: What is a wavefront?
items.expectedAnswer: An imaginary line joining points on a wave that are all in phase (e.g. all crests).
items.explanation: A wavefront connects points in phase, such as a line of crests.
options: An imaginary line joining points on a wave that are all in phase (e.g. all crests).

items.question: What does Huygens' principle state?
items.expectedAnswer: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of new secondary wavelets.
items.explanation: Huygens: each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets that build the next wavefront.
options: Waves always travel in straight lines.
Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of new secondary wavelets.
Light is made only of particles.

items.question: What is diffraction?
items.expectedAnswer: The spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an edge.
items.explanation: Diffraction is the spreading out of waves at an opening or obstacle.
options: The bouncing of waves off a surface.
The change of speed at a boundary.
The spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an edge.

items.question: Diffraction is greatest when the slit width is...
items.expectedAnswer: about the same size as the wavelength.
items.explanation: Maximum diffraction occurs when the gap is comparable to the wavelength.
options: about the same size as the wavelength.

items.question: For a fixed slit width, which waves diffract (spread) MORE?
items.explanation: Longer wavelengths diffract more for the same slit width.

items.question: Does the wavelength of a wave change when it diffracts through a slit?
items.expectedAnswer: No — the wavelength stays the same.
items.explanation: Diffraction changes the wave's direction/spreading but not its wavelength.
options: No — the wavelength stays the same.

items.question: Which types of waves can be diffracted?
items.expectedAnswer: All waves — water, sound and light.
items.explanation: Diffraction is a property of all waves, including water, sound and light.
options: All waves — water, sound and light.

items.question: When a straight water wave passes through a narrow gap, the wavefront on the far side becomes...
items.explanation: Through a narrow gap the wave spreads, producing curved wavefronts (diffraction).

items.question: Why can you hear someone around a corner even if you cannot see them?
items.expectedAnswer: Sound's long wavelength diffracts around the corner more than light does.
items.explanation: Sound has a much longer wavelength than light, so it diffracts (spreads) around corners noticeably.
options: Light cannot travel around corners at all in theory.
Sound's long wavelength diffracts around the corner more than light does.

items.question: A wide opening (much larger than the wavelength) produces...
items.expectedAnswer: very little diffraction (waves pass almost straight through).
items.explanation: When the gap is much larger than the wavelength, diffraction is small.
options: very little diffraction (waves pass almost straight through).

items.question: Two slits, one narrow and one wide, receive the same waves. Which produces more spreading?
items.explanation: Narrower slits (closer to the wavelength) cause more diffraction.

items.question: To increase the diffraction of light through a single slit, you could...
items.expectedAnswer: make the slit narrower or use longer-wavelength (e.g. red) light.
items.explanation: More diffraction comes from a narrower slit and/or a longer wavelength.
options: make the slit narrower or use longer-wavelength (e.g. red) light.

items.question: Red light (longer wavelength) and blue light (shorter wavelength) pass through the same narrow slit. Which diffracts more?
items.explanation: Longer wavelength (red) diffracts more through the same slit.

items.question: According to Huygens' principle, how is the new position of a wavefront found?
items.expectedAnswer: By drawing the envelope (tangent) of all the secondary wavelets.
items.explanation: The new wavefront is the surface that touches (envelopes) all the secondary wavelets.
options: By drawing the envelope (tangent) of all the secondary wavelets.
By counting the number of crests.

items.question: Why is diffraction of light hard to observe in everyday life?
items.expectedAnswer: Light's wavelength is very small, so noticeable diffraction needs a very narrow slit.
items.explanation: Because light's wavelength is tiny, only very narrow gaps produce visible diffraction.
options: Light does not diffract at all.
Light's wavelength is very small, so noticeable diffraction needs a very narrow slit.

items.question: A sound of wavelength 1 m and a beam of light pass through a 1 m wide doorway. Which diffracts noticeably?
items.expectedAnswer: The sound (wavelength similar to the gap).
items.explanation: The sound's wavelength matches the doorway, so it diffracts strongly; light's tiny wavelength barely diffracts.
options: The sound (wavelength similar to the gap).
The light (wavelength similar to the gap).

items.question: Diffraction provides evidence that light behaves as a...
items.explanation: Diffraction is a wave property, supporting the wave model of light.

items.question: As waves pass an obstacle, the bending of the wavefronts around its edges is also a form of...
items.explanation: Waves spreading around the edges of an obstacle is diffraction.

items.question: The degree of diffraction depends on the ratio of...
items.explanation: Diffraction depends on how the wavelength compares with the slit width (λ/width).

items.question: If the slit width equals the wavelength, the diffraction is...
items.explanation: When slit width ≈ wavelength, diffraction is at its most pronounced.

L5.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply Coulomb's Law to the force between point charges

items.question: Which equation is Coulomb's Law?
items.explanation: Coulomb's Law: F = kQ₁Q₂/r² (inverse square of separation).

items.question: Two like charges (both positive) exert what kind of force on each other?
items.explanation: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

items.question: In Coulomb's Law, if the distance between two charges doubles, the force becomes...

items.question: The Coulomb's Law constant k has a value of about...

items.question: Coulomb's Law gives the force as a magnitude. How do you decide its direction?

From whether the charges are like (repel) or unlike (attract).

items.question: What must you convert microcoulombs (µC) to before using Coulomb's Law in SI units?

items.question: Two opposite charges are brought closer together. The attractive force between them...
items.explanation: Smaller r gives a larger force (inverse-square law).

items.question: The force one point charge exerts on another, and the force the second exerts on the first, are...

items.question: Two charges of +4 µC and −4 µC are 2 m apart. Find the magnitude of the force. (k = 9×10⁹)

items.explanation: F ∝ Q₁Q₂, so doubling both multiplies F by 2 × 2 = 4.

items.question: If the distance between two charges is halved, the Coulomb force becomes...
items.explanation: Inverse-square: halving r multiplies F by 1/(½)² = 4.

items.explanation: F ∝ 1/r²: going from 3 m to 1 m multiplies F by (3/1)² = 9, so 2 × 9 = 18 N.

items.question: A +5 µC and a +5 µC charge are 0.5 m apart. Find the force. (k = 9×10⁹)

items.explanation: Use absolute values for the magnitude; the attraction/repulsion gives the direction.
options: The formula uses the sizes of the charges; direction is decided separately.

items.question: Two charges experience a force of 8 N. One charge is then tripled. What is the new force (same distance)?
items.explanation: F ∝ charge, so tripling one charge gives 8 × 3 = 24 N.

items.question: Charge A (+6 µC) and charge B (−2 µC) are 3 m apart. Find the magnitude of the force. (k = 9×10⁹)

items.explanation: For subatomic particles the electrostatic force is vastly stronger than the gravitational force.

items.question: Two charges 4 m apart feel a force of 9 N. If both the distance is halved and one charge doubled, the new force is...
items.explanation: Halving r ×4; doubling one charge ×2; total 9 × 4 × 2 = 72 N.

items.question: What is the electric field 2 m from a +8 µC charge? (k = 9×10⁹)

items.question: What is the force on a 2×10⁻⁶ C charge placed in a field of 5000 N·C⁻¹?
Closer spacing of electric field lines indicates...
items.explanation: Field lines drawn closer together show a stronger electric field.

items.question: The electric field at a point is 6000 N·C⁻¹. What force acts on a −3×10⁻⁶ C charge placed there?

items.question: Two equal positive charges sit on a line. At the exact midpoint between them, the net electric field is...

items.question: Why must you use the SOURCE charge (not the test charge) in E = kQ/r²?

The field is created by the source charge; the test charge only samples it.
Both charges create the same field.

L6.T1.A1.skill_title: Describe the magnetic field of a current-carrying conductor and solenoid

items.question: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire?

items.question: A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field similar to that of a...

items.question: What happens to the magnetic field direction if the current in a wire is reversed?

items.question: Adding an iron core to a solenoid does what to its magnetic field?

items.question: An advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet is that...

items.question: Using the right-hand rule, if conventional current flows upward in a vertical wire, the field on the wire's left side (facing it) points...

items.question: Two parallel wires carry current in the SAME direction. They tend to...
items.explanation: Parallel currents in the same direction attract (their fields interact).
options: have no effect on each other.

items.question: How can you reverse the poles of a solenoid electromagnet?
items.expectedAnswer: Reverse the direction of the current.
items.explanation: Reversing the current swaps the north and south poles of the solenoid.

items.question: Compared with a single straight wire, why is a solenoid's field stronger and more uniform inside?

The fields of many turns add together inside the coil.

items.question: An electromagnet is used in a scrapyard crane. Why is an electromagnet better than a permanent magnet here?

items.question: If the number of turns on a solenoid is doubled (same current), the magnetic field strength roughly...
items.explanation: More turns per length increases the field strength of the solenoid.

items.question: The magnetic field lines inside a solenoid point from...
items.expectedAnswer: its south pole to its north pole (inside), completing the loop.

items.question: What evidence shows that a current-carrying wire has a magnetic field?

items.question: Two parallel wires carry current in OPPOSITE directions. They tend to...

using a battery to make a magnet.

items.question: Electromagnetic induction converts...

items.question: A stronger magnet moved through a coil at the same speed induces an EMF that is...

items.question: Induced EMF depends on the RATE of change of flux. This means EMF is larger when the flux changes...

items.question: Why is no EMF induced when a magnet rests motionless beside a coil?

items.question: Why does spinning a coil faster in a generator produce a higher EMF?
